title: A bubble, a mirage (167–171)
hook: look on the world as a bubble, as a mirage, and the king of death won't see you
tomorrow: The moon from behind a cloud (172–178)

segments.voice: Yesterday, no one can purify another: by oneself harm is done, by oneself one is purified. Your line was no one can do it for you. What step did you take yourself? Day one hundred ninety-one, and chapter thirteen begins: the world.
screen: `NO ONE CAN DO IT FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: Blow a soap bubble on a sunny day and watch it. For a second or two it holds the whole world on its skin: the sky, the trees, your own stretched face, all swirling in rainbow colors. It's real. You can see it. And then, with no sound at all, it's gone. Or drive down a highway in the summer heat and watch the shimmering pool on the road ahead that never gets any closer. Real shimmer, no water. Chapter thirteen of the Dhammapada takes those two sights and hands them to you as glasses to see through. Today: a bubble, a mirage.
screen: `A SOAP BUBBLE IN THE SUN.` → `WATER ON THE HIGHWAY THAT ISN'T.` → `TWO SIGHTS TO SEE THROUGH.`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with a wake-up call, verse one sixty-eight: "Rouse thyself! do not be idle! Follow the law of virtue!" The commentary says the Buddha spoke it when he first came home to his father's city and walked the streets with his alms bowl. His father, the king, was mortified to see his son begging, and hurried to stop him. The Buddha answered that going for alms was the custom of his lineage, the lineage of Buddhas, and spoke this verse. Then comes today's line, verse one seventy: "Look upon the world as a bubble, look upon it as a mirage: the king of death does not see him who thus looks down upon the world." In Pali, a bubble is pubbuḷa, and a mirage is marīcikā. Neither is nothing. A bubble really shimmers; a mirage really shines. What they aren't is solid or lasting. That's the way of looking the verse asks for. Not that the world doesn't matter, but that nothing in it will hold still or hold your weight forever. And the verse's promise is plain: the king of death does not see the one who looks at the world this way. Verse one seventy-one adds a picture: the world is like a glittering royal chariot; fools sink into it, the wise don't cling. A Mahayana text, the Diamond Sutra, closes with a list of similes in the same spirit, among them a dream, a bubble, dew and lightning. Two very different texts, one shared image.
screen: `ROUSE YOURSELF: THE KING'S SON BEGS.` · `PUBBUḶA AND MARĪCIKĀ.` · `REAL, BUT NOT SOLID.` · `A DREAM, A BUBBLE, DEW.` · then, large: `A BUBBLE, A MIRAGE.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at something that shimmers: bubbles in a glass of sparkling water, light on a window, your reflection in a dark screen. If not, just picture one soap bubble floating in front of you. Watch it without trying to catch it. Notice the colors moving on its skin. Then close your eyes and watch your thoughts the same way: each one shimmering, real for a moment, and then gone, with no sound. Nothing to catch. Just watching. The bell holds the time.
A bubble. Verse one seventy: look upon the world as a bubble, as a mirage: shining, real for a moment, never solid.
Your line: a bubble, a mirage. Today, when something small feels huge, a comment, a price, a worry, see it as a bubble for a moment, and watch what happens to its weight. Day one hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Buddhists across many schools reflect on impermanence with images like the bubble, the mirage and the dream, often in chanting or in teachings given at funerals.

match.prompt: match each image to what it teaches.
pairs: real for a moment, then gone

myth: the verse says the world doesn't matter at all
a bubble really shimmers; the point is that nothing in the world is solid or lasting.
the Diamond Sutra uses a bubble among its images too
its closing verse includes a dream, a bubble, dew and lightning.
the commentary links verse 168 to the Buddha's first return home
his father was mortified to see him begging for alms in the streets.

fork.setup: you're the king. your son, now the Buddha, has come home and is walking your city's streets with a begging bowl. what do you do?
options: hurry out to stop him; a prince doesn't beg.
hide in the palace and pretend not to see.
join him with a bowl of your own.
fork.reveal: the commentary says the king rushed to stop him. the Buddha answered that alms-round is the custom of the Buddhas' lineage, and spoke verse 168.

original.note: Pali: a mirage — the shimmer of heat that looks like water; paired with pubbuḷa, a bubble, in verse 170.

trapdoor: what you thought: the world is an illusion, so nothing matters.
what it means: the world is real like a bubble is real: bright, brief, never solid enough to lean on.
what a scholar hears: pubbuḷa and marīcikā in verse 170; Müller's 'king of death' renders maccurājā, and the Diamond Sutra's closing verse carries the same image.
